--- title: "Setting the stage" format: html: toc: true revealjs: slide-number: true toc: false code-fold: false code-tools: true smaller: true execute: echo: true --- ## A simple data science problem {.smaller} - We have a dataset and a target. - We want to build a simple baseline model to find out if there is signal in the data. - We are going to use regular pandas and scikit-learn to pre-process and train on the data. - For the sake of the example, we will use a **linear model**. ## Load and explore the data ::: {#8ac50a97 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd import numpy as np X = pd.read_csv("../data/employee_salaries/data.csv") y = pd.read_csv("../data/employee_salaries/target.csv")["current_annual_salary"] X.head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Explore the target Let's take a look at the target: ::: {#009fd53a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} y.head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0 69222.18 1 97392.47 2 104717.28 3 52734.57 4 93396.00 Name: current_annual_salary, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: This is a **regression** task: we want to predict the value of `current_annual_salary`. ## Strategizing We can begin by exploring the dataframe with `.describe`, and then think of a plan for pre-processing our data. ::: {#493a87d1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} X.describe(include="all") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
gender department department_name division assignment_category employee_position_title date_first_hired year_first_hired

25% NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 1998.000000
50% NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 2005.000000
75% NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 2012.000000
max NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 2016.000000
``` ::: ::: ## Our plan We need to: - Impute some missing values in the `gender` column. - Encode convert categorical features into numerical features. - Convert the column `date_first_hired` into numerical features. - Scale numerical features. - Evaluate the performance of the model. ## Step 1: Convert date features to numerical {.smaller} We extract numerical features from the `date_first_hired` column. ::: {#1a17fdf9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create a copy to work with X_processed = X.copy() # Parse the date column X_processed['date_first_hired'] = pd.to_datetime(X_processed['date_first_hired']) # Extract numerical features from date X_processed['hired_month'] = X_processed['date_first_hired'].dt.month X_processed['hired_year'] = X_processed['date_first_hired'].dt.year # Drop original date column X_processed = X_processed.drop('date_first_hired', axis=1) print("Features after date transformation:") print("\nShape:", X_processed.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Features after date transformation: Shape: (9228, 9) ``` ::: ::: ## Step 2: Encode categorical features {.smaller} We encode the categorical features using one-hot encoding. ::: {#e3d6221e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Find the categorical columns categorical_cols = X_processed.select_dtypes(include=['object']).columns.tolist() print("Categorical columns to encode:", categorical_cols) # Apply one-hot encoding only to categorical columns X_encoded = pd.get_dummies(X_processed, columns=categorical_cols) print("\nShape after encoding:", X_encoded.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Categorical columns to encode: ['gender', 'department', 'department_name', 'division', 'assignment_category', 'employee_position_title'] Shape after encoding: (9228, 1218) ``` ::: ::: ## Step 3: Impute missing values {.smaller auto-animate="true"} Some models cannot handle missing values. We impute the missing values in the `gender` column: ::: {#1277075d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer # Impute missing values with most frequent value imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent') X_encoded_imputed = pd.DataFrame( imputer.fit_transform(X_encoded), columns=X_encoded.columns ) ``` ::: ## Step 3: Impute missing values {auto-animate="true"} ::: {.callout-important} Missing values are important! The fact that a value is missing is by itself useful information, and the pattern of missingness is also important. For this reason, skrub transformers keep missing values as they are to retain the information content. ::: Example: - A dataset about **employment** has the column **current position**. - A missing value in **current position** likely indicates **unemployment** - Imputing **current position** with "most frequent" would lead to incorrect assumptions about the data. ## Step 4: Scale numerical features {.smaller} - Some models work better when all the numeric features have comparable scale. - `RidgeCV` is one of them, so we need to scale numerical features. - `SquashingScaler` is an improvement over the `RobustScaler` ::: {#a78e3a96 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from skrub import SquashingScaler # Initialize the scaler scaler = SquashingScaler() # Fit and transform the data X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_encoded_imputed) X_scaled = pd.DataFrame(X_scaled, columns=X_encoded_imputed.columns) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} Outliers (values very far from the mean) make scaling hard to do. **Robust scaling** may be needed. ::: ## Step 5: Train Ridge model with cross-validation {.smaller} Train a `RidgeCV` regression model and evaluate with cross-validation. ::: {#f2cc9d72 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, cross_validate import numpy as np # Initialize Ridge model ridge = RidgeCV() # Perform cross-validation (5-fold) results_ridge = cross_validate(ridge, X_scaled, y, cv=5, scoring=["r2"]) # Display results print("Cross-Validation Results:") print( f"Mean test R²: {results_ridge['test_r2'].mean():.4f} (+/- {results_ridge['test_r2'].std():.4f})" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cross-Validation Results: Mean test R²: 0.8931 (+/- 0.0222) ``` ::: ::: ## - So much boilerplate! - What happened to the training split? - Was there leakage? - A lot of code to write and remember => mistakes are more likely ## Intermission: data leakage and fit/transform {auto-animate="true"} ::: {#c510829f .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer df = pd.DataFrame({ "value": [1, 3, None, 5, 10, None, 1000, 5] }) df_train = df[:5] df_test = df[5:] ``` ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {#8d8d791a .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_train ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
value
0 1.0
1 3.0
2 NaN
3 5.0
4 10.0
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {#ad37e1c9 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_test ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
value
5 NaN
6 1000.0
7 5.0
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Intermission: data leakage and fit/transform {auto-animate="true"} What happens if you try to find the mean over all data? ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {#8260e2be .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="mean").set_output(transform="pandas") df_imputed = imputer.fit_transform(df) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} ![](images/fit-transform-impute-1.png) ::: ::: ## Intermission: data leakage and fit/transform {auto-animate="true"} The proper way to do it: fit the transformer on the training data, transform the training with the same mean: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {#4e241107 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(imputer.fit(df_train).transform(df_test)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` value 5 4.75 6 1000.00 7 5.00 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} ![](images/fit-transform-impute-2.png) ![](images/fit-transform-impute-3.png) ::: ::: ## "Just ask an agent to write the code" {.smaller} ::: {.incremental} - Operations were in the wrong order. - The datetime feature was treated like a categorical feature (and **one-hot encoded**). - Cells could not be executed in order without proper debugging and re-prompting. - `pd.get_dummies` was executed on the full dataframe, rather than only on the training split, leading to **data leakage**. ::: ## The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science ![https://trl-lab.github.io/ds-agent-failures/](images/pct_pipelines_with_failure.svg) > Almost every agentic DS pipeline contains at least one failure mode, regardless of the agent scaffold or the underlying model. ::: {.fragment} ::: {.callout-important} We want to minimize the chance of making mistakes. ::: ::: ## skrub to the rescue {.smaller} Thankfully, we can `import skrub`: ::: {#a931e505 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} from skrub import tabular_pipeline # Perform cross-validation (5-fold) results_tp = cross_validate(tabular_pipeline("regression"), X, y, cv=5, scoring=["r2"]) # Display results print("Cross-Validation Results:") print( f"tabular_pipeline: Mean test R²: {results_tp['test_r2'].mean():.4f} (+/- {results_tp['test_r2'].std():.4f})" ) print( f"Ridge: Mean test R²: {results_ridge['test_r2'].mean():.4f} (+/- {results_ridge['test_r2'].std():.4f})" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cross-Validation Results: tabular_pipeline: Mean test R²: 0.9111 (+/- 0.0136) Ridge: Mean test R²: 0.8931 (+/- 0.0222) ``` ::: ::: ## What's in the `tabular_pipeline` ![](images/tabular-pipeline.png){fig-align="center"} And **good defaults**! ## Pre-processing is part of the pipeline! {.smaller} - There isn't a clear separation between "pre-processing", "feature engineering" and "learning". ::: {.fragment} - If you learn something while pre-processing your training data ("this is a datetime"), you need to apply that knowledge to the test data. ::: ::: {.fragment} - This is why skrub provides **transformers**, rather than **functions**: transformers are stateful and can be used in pipelines, functions are not. ::: ## What we saw in this chapter - We built a predictive pipeline using traditional tools - We talked about missing data imputation - We discussed data leakage - We tested skrub's `tabular_pipeline` - We covered why pre-processing is part of the pipeline ## Machine learning with dataframes: why skrub - skrub provides tools to build robust pipelines - this is done by bringing pre-processing and feature engineering __inside__ of the pipeline - robust code avoids boilerplate - the fit/transform framework builds production-ready pipelines - skrub transformers are tuned to use **good defaults** ## Course Roadmap 1. Data exploration with skrub's `TableReport` 2. Data cleaning and sanitization with the `Cleaner` 3. Column-based operations with `ApplyToCols` 4. Selectors and how to use them for advanced column selection 5. Automatic feature engineering with the `TableVectorizer` 6. A robust baseline for machine learning tasks with the `tabular_pipeline` 7. Beyond pipelines: skrub Data Ops
